note: The hybrid-parity oracle. Each program is planned with planHybrid for the dialect, its SQL
prefix is EXECUTED on a real server through the runner executeHybrid is handed, and the answer must
equal what SEL answers for the whole program over the same rows loaded as the context (run()).
The contract this holds a plan to (docs/internals/sql-translation.md 12.1):
* the value is run()'s -- same rows in the same order, and, for a hybrid plan, the same keys
(a pure_sql plan answers a ROWSET: its rows are numbered 1..n by the database, so only the
rows and their order are compared);
* the error is run()'s -- same code and position -- or the plan is pure_memory: an error SEL raises
on a row that a LIMIT or WHERE would have cut must not disappear;
* the caller's context is not mutated by executeHybrid, whatever the classification (SQL cannot
perform a helper's assignment, so no plan promises it), and unrelated variables are preserved;
* every program that observes an order names a UNIQUE ORDER BY key: nothing here relies on a
`expect` guards the corpus against a shared bug: it is what SEL must answer, derived by hand from the
fixture (eight orders, ids 1..8, customers 7 7 9 9 11 11 12 12): `fields` are the values of a field
down the result rows, `keys` the result's keys, `error` the code run() must raise.

ORDERS.query: SELECT id, customer_id, amount, name FROM hy_orders ORDER BY id

CUSTOMERS.query: SELECT id, name FROM hy_customers ORDER BY id

programs.name: keys.filter-then-key-reader-map
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> FILTER(_["id"] > 5) .> MAP(RECORD("k", _K, "i", _["id"], "z", COUNT(SPLIT(_["name"], "a"))))
programs.note: FILTER keeps the ordinals of the sorted list (6, 7, 8); a continuation that reads `_K` after a split must see them, not the rows' ordinals in the SQL rowset.

programs.name: keys.filter-then-unsupported-filter
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> FILTER(_["id"] > 5) .> FILTER(COUNT(SPLIT(_["name"], "a")) > 1)
programs.note: The result keys are part of the value: the one row that survives is `6`, not `1`.

programs.name: keys.take-filter-filter
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> TAKE(6) .> FILTER(_["id"] > 2) .> FILTER(COUNT(SPLIT(_["name"], "a")) > 1)
programs.note: TAKE renumbers, FILTER then keeps the renumbered ordinals: 3, 5, 6.

programs.name: keys.pure-sql-rowset
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> FILTER(_["id"] > 6)
programs.note: A pure_sql plan answers a rowset: its rows are numbered 1..n by the database, where run() keeps the FILTER's ordinals (7, 8). The contract compares rows in order and not the keys of a pure_sql result (docs/internals/sql-translation.md 12.1, 'row keys').

programs.name: keys.take-renumbers-so-the-split-is-safe
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> FILTER(_["id"] > 2) .> TAKE(3) .> MAP(RECORD("k", _K))
programs.note: TAKE renumbers from 1, so `_K` after it is 1, 2, 3 whoever computed the rows.

programs.name: keys.filter-then-renumbering-map
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> FILTER(_["id"] > 5) .> MAP(RECORD("z", COUNT(SPLIT(_["name"], "a"))))
programs.note: A step that renumbers hides the FILTER's keys, so the split after the FILTER is invisible: keys 1..3.

programs.name: context.continuation-reads-the-callers-names
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> FILTER(COUNT(SPLIT(_["name"], "a")) > LIM)
programs.note: The continuation reads LIM from the caller's context, as run() does. Go replaced the context with an empty record.

programs.name: context.literal-helper
programs.sel: N = 1 + 1; ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> TAKE(N) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"], "z", COUNT(SPLIT(_["name"], "a"))))
programs.note: A helper folding to a literal is inlined at its read.

programs.name: context.non-literal-helper-read-by-the-continuation
programs.sel: H = LEN(ENCODE_BASE64(TO_UTF8("abc"))); ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"], "z", COUNT(SPLIT(_["name"], "a")) + H)) .> TAKE(2)
programs.note: A helper the continuation reads stays an assignment in front of the steps and is evaluated once. The caller's context must not gain it.

programs.name: error.take-after-a-map-that-can-raise
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"], "z", IF(_["id"] > 4, ABORT("x"), 1))) .> TAKE(2)
programs.note: run() evaluates the MAP body on every row before TAKE cuts: row 5 raises. A plan that pushes the LIMIT past the MAP's local half hides it.

programs.name: error.drop-after-a-map-that-can-raise
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"], "z", IF(_["id"] > 4, ABORT("x"), 1))) .> DROP(1)
programs.note: The same with DROP.

programs.name: error.sort-and-take-after-a-map-that-can-raise
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"], "z", IF(_["id"] > 4, ABORT("x"), 1))) .> SORT_BY(_["i"], "DESC") .> TAKE(1)
programs.note: A re-sort and a limit behind the MAP cannot make row 5 disappear.

programs.name: error.missing-key-in-a-sort-behind-a-filter
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["nokey"]) .> FILTER(_["customer_id"] == 7) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"]))
programs.note: A sort key no row has is E_NO_KEY even when the FILTER after it would keep nothing.

programs.name: error.control-filter-before-the-map
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> FILTER(_["id"] < 3) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"], "z", IF(_["id"] > 4, ABORT("x"), 1)))
programs.note: CONTROL: rows 3.. never reach the MAP, so nothing raises, in SEL and in a plan alike.

programs.name: error.control-take-before-the-map
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> TAKE(2) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"], "z", IF(_["id"] > 4, ABORT("x"), 1)))
programs.note: CONTROL: the TAKE is written before the MAP, so the plan may push it.

programs.name: order.bucket-follows-the-explicit-sort
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["customer_id"], "DESC") .> BUCKET(_["customer_id"], RECORD("c", _K, "n", COUNT(_)))
programs.note: Groups appear in the order the sort put their first member. The SQL dropped the sort's ORDER BY around the GROUP BY.

programs.name: order.bucket-after-a-descending-sort-then-map
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"], "DESC") .> BUCKET(_["customer_id"]) .> MAP(RECORD("c", _K, "n", COUNT(_)))
programs.note: Memory gives 12, 11, 9, 7; the statement grouped in ascending key order.

programs.name: order.link-after-a-sort
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"], "DESC") .> LINK(CUSTOMERS, O, C, O["customer_id"] == C["id"]) .> MAP(RECORD("o", _["O"]["id"], "n", _["C"]["name"])) .> TAKE(3)
programs.note: The ORDER BY of the sort must survive the join and the limit.

programs.name: order.stable-ties-across-a-select-cols
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["name"], "DESC") .> SELECT_COLS("id", "customer_id") .> TOP_BY(_["customer_id"], "DESC", 2)
programs.note: Customer 12 is rows 8 (foxtrot) and 7 (echo); the sort by name put 8 first and SEL's TOP_BY keeps ties in that order. A database that discards the inner ORDER BY may answer 7, 8.

programs.name: order.distinct-after-a-sort-on-an-unprojected-column
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["amount"]) .> MAP(RECORD("c", _["customer_id"])) .> DISTINCT
programs.note: SELECT DISTINCT with an ORDER BY column that is not in the select list is invalid on PostgreSQL. The plan must run and answer 11, 12, 7, 9 (first appearances in amount order).

programs.name: order.bucket-first-appearance-with-ties
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["amount"]) .> BUCKET(_["customer_id"], RECORD("c", _K, "n", COUNT(_)))
programs.note: Amounts 3 4 5 7 8 9 10 12 belong to customers 11 12 7 9 11 12 7 9.

programs.name: order.two-sorts-tie-order
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> SORT_BY(_["customer_id"], "DESC") .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"]))
programs.note: The later sort's keys come first, the earlier sort breaks ties (docs 12.1).

programs.name: binder.helper-named-like-the-explicit-binder-sort
programs.sel: N = 5; ORDERS .> FILTER(_["id"] > 1) .> SORT_BY(N, N["id"], "DESC") .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"]))
programs.note: The literal helper N must not be inlined into the binder position.

programs.name: binder.helper-named-like-the-explicit-binder-bucket
programs.sel: N = 5; ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> FILTER(_["id"] > 1) .> BUCKET(N, N["customer_id"], RECORD("c", _K, "n", COUNT(N)))
programs.note: The four-argument BUCKET.

programs.name: binder.helper-named-like-the-explicit-binder-top-by
programs.sel: N = 5; ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> TOP_BY(N, N["id"], "DESC", 2) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"]))
programs.note: The five-argument TOP_BY.

programs.name: binder.helper-named-like-the-explicit-binder-link
programs.sel: O = 5; ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> LINK(CUSTOMERS, O, C, O["customer_id"] == C["id"]) .> MAP(RECORD("o", _["O"]["id"], "c", _["C"]["name"]))
programs.note: The five-argument LINK.

programs.name: binder.split-before-a-link-keeps-the-left-name
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> TAKE(4) .> LINK(CUSTOMERS, _1["customer_id"] == _2["id"] AND COUNT(SPLIT(_1["name"], "a")) > 0) .> MAP(RECORD("n", _["ORDERS"]["name"], "c", _["CUSTOMERS"]["name"]))
programs.note: The unrenderable predicate keeps the LINK in memory behind a SQL prefix; the joined row must still carry the left side under ORDERS (spec 7.4), not `_INPUT`.

programs.name: context.pure-memory-plan-does-not-mutate-the-caller
programs.sel: A = 1; A += 1; ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> TAKE(A) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"]))
programs.note: Stage 1 refuses a compound assignment, so this is a pure_memory plan: run()'s assignments would leave A in the caller's context. executeHybrid never mutates the caller's context, whatever the classification (a SQL prefix cannot perform a helper's assignment, so the contract cannot promise it for the others).

programs.name: context.helper-assignment-in-a-split-plan-does-not-leak
programs.sel: T = "x"; ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> MAP(RECORD("i", _["id"], "x", COUNT(SPLIT(_["name"], T)))) .> TAKE(2)
programs.note: A helper the continuation reads is assigned inside the continuation's private context; the caller's context does not gain T.

programs.name: binder.self-join-does-not-shadow-the-right-side
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> TAKE(4) .> LINK(ORDERS, O, P, O["id"] + 4 == P["id"] AND COUNT(SPLIT(O["name"], "a")) > 0) .> MAP(RECORD("o", _["O"]["id"], "p", _["P"]["id"]))
programs.note: The left side of a LINK is the truncated prefix and the right side is the WHOLE relation of the same name. A continuation that rebinds the source name to the SQL rows before the LINK would also replace the right side, and the join would find no partner for rows 1-4 in ids 5-8 (gate fuzz seed 20260905: only Go kept such a program in memory).

programs.name: order.bucket-over-sorted-and-limited
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"], "DESC") .> TAKE(6) .> BUCKET(_["customer_id"], RECORD("c", _K, "n", COUNT(_)))
programs.note: A LIMIT beside the ORDER BY keeps WHICH rows survive, not the order a GROUP BY over them returns its groups in: SEL lists the groups in the order their first member appears in the sorted list (12, 11, 9). No host may push the BUCKET into SQL (gate review; see sql/cases 51 stmt.order.*): the sorted, limited rows come from the database and the grouping runs in memory.

programs.name: binder.link-later-in-the-continuation-keeps-the-left-name
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["id"]) .> TAKE(4) .> FILTER(COUNT(SPLIT(_["name"], "a")) > 0) .> LINK(CUSTOMERS, _1["customer_id"] == _2["id"]) .> MAP(RECORD("n", _["ORDERS"]["name"], "c", _["CUSTOMERS"]["name"]))
programs.note: The split falls before the FILTER (SPLIT has no SQL), so the LINK is not the first step of the continuation. A joined row names its left side after the variable its pipeline STARTED from (spec 7.4): the continuation is fed `_INPUT`, so a host that renames the source only when the LINK comes first would answer E_NO_KEY on `_[\"ORDERS\"]` where run() answers.

programs.name: order.filter-after-sort-keeps-the-order
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["amount"]) .> FILTER(_["amount"] > 4)
programs.note: The sort is by amount, so the answer is NOT in id order. The FILTER's WHERE goes beside the ORDER BY in the same select: wrapped in a derived table with no LIMIT the servers drop the ORDER BY and return the rows in no order (Rust-lane audit).

programs.name: order.projection-then-filter-of-sorted-rows-keeps-the-order
programs.sel: ORDERS .> SORT_BY(_["amount"]) .> MAP(RECORD("a", _["amount"], "i", _["id"])) .> FILTER(_["a"] > 4)
programs.note: A projection between the sort and the filter cannot avoid the wrap, so the statement is refused and the plan keeps the sorted rows in SQL and filters in memory; the order survives.

bounded.name: planning.nested-calls-are-linear
bounded.note: The planner visited every call's arguments twice, so time doubled per level of nesting; 40 levels must plan in well under a second.
